slides.title: Device Sign-In
slides.subtitle: Sign in on the company's page when the agent cannot take a browser callback
slides.notes: Some personal agents run in a terminal or on a device with no browser callback. Device Sign-In lets the user sign in on the company's page with a link and a code, while the agent polls politely for the result.

slides.title: Why Device Sign-In
slides.statement: The user signs in **elsewhere**. The agent **waits**, at the company's pace.
slides.notes: The user opens a link on any device and types a short code. Meanwhile the agent asks the company whether sign-in is done, never faster than the company allows.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model"] subgraph USR["User, any device"] direction TB P["User"] end subgraph HOST["Your host, trusted"] direction TB T["Agent tool
read-only"] -- "begin" --> S["DeviceSignInClient"] S -- "device code,
Account Token" --> V[("Reactor stores")] end subgraph CO["Company"] direction TB C["Company API"] --- G["Sign-in page"] end HOST -- "link and user code" --> USR USR -- "signs in" --> CO HOST -- "polls, Session Key proofs" --> CO HOST -. "evidence, opaque reference" .-> M
slides.caption: The user code is for the user; the device code and the tokens never leave the host's stores.
slides.notes: Three zones and the model. In your host, the read-only agent tool asks the DeviceSignInClient to begin, and the client keeps the private device code, and later the Account Token, in Reactor stores. The host shows the user a link and a short code. The user signs in on the company's page, from any device. Meanwhile the host polls the company, each poll with a fresh DPoP proof signed with the Session Key; the first poll binds the device code to that key, so only this Session can finish the sign-in. Off to the side, the model receives lifecycle evidence and an opaque token reference, nothing secret.

slides.title: Starting

items.title: Begin
items.detail: For an existing Session, named by its Session Key

items.title: Authorize
items.detail: Link, user code, interval, private device code

items.title: Hand off
items.detail: The user opens the link and enters the code

slides.notes: The client asks the company for a device authorization on the Session that already exists. The company returns a link, a user code, a polling interval and a private device code. The client checks the link is on the issuer's host or one of its protected_resources. The device code goes into a Reactor store; the tool gets the link, the code and an opaque reference.

slides.title: Polling at the company's pace

items.title: Too early
items.detail: No request: the interval has not passed

items.title: Signed in
items.detail: Same Session, Account Token, partial scopes

slides.notes: A poll before the interval sends nothing. Then the company says pending, then slow down, and the client adds five seconds to its interval. Every poll that goes out carries a fresh DPoP proof, signed with the same Session Key. Finally the same Session comes back signed in, with an Account Token and one requested scope missing.

slides.title: The sign-in lifecycle
slides.diagram:
stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  state "Signed out" as SO
  state "Waiting" as W
  state "Polling" as P
  state "Signed in" as SI
  [*] --> SO
  SO --> W : link and code shown
  W --> W : too early, no request
  W --> P : interval passed
  P --> W : authorization_pending
  P --> W : slow_down, plus 5 s
  P --> SI : same Session upgraded
slides.caption: One Session from start to end: signed out, waiting at the company's pace, then signed in.
slides.notes: Follow the Session from the left. It starts signed out, and begins waiting once the link and code have been shown to the user. A poll before the interval sends no request at all. When the interval has passed the client polls: authorization_pending sends it back to waiting, and slow_down does too, with five seconds added to the interval. Finally the company answers signed in, and it is the original Session that is upgraded, not a new one: the token response carries no Session ID, because the proof's key names the Session. The tool's result is evidence of exactly these steps, including the one requested scope that was left out and reported.

slides.title: What stays where

right.heading: What the model sees
items: The link and user code, as shown

slides.notes: The user code is meant for the user; the device code is not, and never leaves the host. Tokens, assertions and proofs stay host-only too.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The Pydantic AI and Agent Runtimes examples run the real state machine against a deterministic company
slides.notes: The company in the examples always answers pending, then slow down, so every rule is exercised on each run. The Device Sign-In guide covers the production setup.
